newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Best on Ground - Andrew Bartram's Aussie Rules Column - AFL.
newsitem.headline: Best on Ground - Andrew Bartram's Aussie Rules Column - AFL.

text.p: By Andrew Bartram*
STATE OF ORIGIN: STATE OF FLUX?
State-of-origin football was traditionally one of the jewels in the AFL crown but the league is fast discovering that diamonds aren't forever.

The league is believed to be considering playing future origin series every two years to relieve injury-hit clubs and to free-up a weekend on the alternate year, allowing clubs the luxury of a mid-season bye.
Careful not to deprive the football public its voracious appetite for the game, one round would be played over two weekends.

The proposal might rejuvinate interest in the origin concept which was struck a blow when the competition was nationalised in 1992 and may well have died three years later with its champion, Ted Whitten.
State-of-origin football has lost its mass appeal because it no longer has any real novelty value and state parochialism at AFL level has waned considerably.
OPINION DIVIDED
The honour of state representation and playing with the best footballers is an enormous incentive for players, as the quality of the football would attest.

St Kilda ruck-rover and perennial Victorian star Robert Harvey told The Age newspaper that footballers didn't get the opportunity to play international sport and therefore state-of-origin was the pinnacle.
"The footy is fantastic. I think it lifts to another level," he said.
During the week however North Melbourne and West Coast called on the AFL to scrap origin football.
In a submission to the league, North's chief executive, Greg Miller, said: "I just don't like the fact that, given the money we pay these players, we lose control of them completely for a week".
Even Victorian chairman of selectors Gerard Healy said there was nothing in origin football for the clubs except the possibility of losing players.
And that is the nub of the argument against state-of-origin football.

Clubs and supporters don't see origin as a celebration of the game. They see it as a superfluous and dangerous AFL indulgence. For them, the premiership season is paramount and, as all coaches will concede and Essendon has demonstrated, injuries determine the course of a season.
THE GAME GOES ON

Tonight at Subiaco Oval Western Australia will be looking to regain state football credibility with a win over the Allies, the team comprised of players from Tasmania and the minor football states and territories.
Last time the teams met in 1995 the fledgling Allies upset the Sandgropers who were criticised for perceived apathy and complacency in their approach to the game.
Coach Ross Glendinning has named a strong line-up which should turn the tables on an Allies team deprived through injury of superstars Wayne Carey, James Hird, Paul Kelly and Jason Dunstall.

Bookies can't split South Australia and Victoria who meet at Football Park on Saturday night. On paper the Vics look stronger but the Crow-eaters always rise to the state-of-origin occasion and will be spurred on by 45,000 fans baying for Victorian blood.

The South Australian half forward line looks particularly potent with the wizardry of Darren Jarman and Michael O'Loughlin on the flanks and the powerful marking Nick Holland at centre half forward. His duel with Michael Sexton will be pivotal.
Maybe the Vics will "stick it up 'em" one last time for Teddy and win a thriller.
*Andrew Bartram is a freelance sports writer who writes a regular AFL column for Reuters. Any comments please mark to his attention and send to cybercafe@ca.com.au
